newsitem.title: FRANCE: Italian veteran Rosi says Cannes an assembly line.
newsitem.headline: Italian veteran Rosi says Cannes an assembly line.

text.p: "I haven't even got time to grab a coffee. Cannes has become an assembly line," complained Italian maestro Francesco Rosi as he tackled yet another festival interview.

With "The Truce" in competition for the top Golden Palm award, the veteran director is back in the French Riviera to show the film, which is based on Primo Levi's harrowing account of his epic journey homewards after surviving a Nazi death-camp.
Rosi, a regular in Cannes, who made Palm-winner "The Mattei Case" and "Christ Stopped at Eboli" among others, said 50th festival had little in common with the golden years of the 60s.

"Today there is no time for a calm lunch. I have to do a string of interviews and I try not to say the same things every time because otherwise I feel a cretin," the forceful 74-year-old told Reuters.

"Cannes has changed because cinema has changed. The mood used to be much more relaxed. Today a movie has become a much more elaborate object -- not artistically but technically -- and we need the market more and more," he said.
Festival critics gave "The Truce" a lukewarm reception, saying it paled in comparison to the moral power of Levi's "The Truce", published in 1963.

John Turturro, Cannes best actor for "Barton Fink", plays Levi as he emerges, racked by scarlet fever and almost mute, from the Auschwitz camp and zig-zags home to Turin through a Europe devastated by war.

Industry magazine Variety criticised the film as a "pedestrian adaptation condensing Levi's experience into an episodic series of picaresque and poignant vignettes that fails to convey the vast human canvas or the emotional impact of (the book)."
Rosi said that he quickly ruled out tackling Levi's first book, "If This is a Man" which the former World War Two partisan wrote just after his release from Auschwitz.
"I didn't think of doing a film on the extermination camps after the movies that have already been done on the subject, because I believed I had nothing new to say," he said.
"'The Truce' focus on the possibility of regaining confidence, in the knowledge that the threat is always there. 'There is always a war'," says one of the characters in the film."

With a passion for the darker side of man's soul -- bandits in "Salvatre Giuliano", Mafiosi in "Lucky Luciano" and "Illustrious Corpses", crooked politicians in "Hands Across the City" -- Rosi said his latest work had completely absorbed him and he needed time to recover.
"I have several ideas but no concrete projects. I need to emerge from this film in which I got so involved," he said.
Italian directors have been prominent in this year's festival line-up, including Marco Bellochio's costume drama "The Prince of Hamburg" and Gabriele Salvatores' cyber-space "Nirvana".
"There is talent around, and directors are interested in the reality around us in the best tradition of Italian cinema.

"But these lads need a different discipline as far as funding goes so that they can work better with the ambition of doing something bigger than small-theme or funny films which earn money quickly," Rosi said.
